title: College or Career? On False Positives and Negatives
author: Matthew Carr
source: Thomas B. Fordham Institute, Flypaper (fordhaminstitute.org), September 17, 2026
summary: Matthew Carr, writing for the Fordham Institute, welcomes the backlash against 'college for all' but warns that the multiple-pathways movement risks overcorrecting by treating modest grades and test scores as proof that students should avoid a four-year degree. His central analytic move is to frame post-secondary advising as a trade-off between two errors: false positives, where students are pushed into college and drop out with debt, and false negatives, where students who would have completed and benefited are steered away. Regression-discontinuity studies from Texas and Georgia show that students just above admissions cutoffs gained substantially in degree attainment and earnings, suggesting that a lower predicted completion probability does not imply lower expected returns. Because the long-run costs of the two errors can differ sharply, Carr argues that any readiness threshold simply shifts the balance of mistakes, so prediction alone cannot decide the right path for an individual. He points instead to structured advising, citing Bottom Line and an 18-week Michigan college-planning course, and to Kahneman's idea of decision hygiene, recommending that advisers break the decision into components and keep multiple pathways open as long as possible.
points: Any rule for sorting students into post-secondary paths produces both false positives (college recommended, student drops out) and false negatives (student discouraged who would have succeeded), and recent debate has focused almost entirely on the first.

Texas students just above university admissions cutoffs raised bachelor's attainment by about 12 percentage points and earnings by about 8 percent, and Georgia's comparable estimate was roughly 17 percent higher household income by age 30.

A student's 50 percent predicted completion probability says little on its own; the right choice also depends on accessible colleges, aid, supports, opportunity costs, and the real alternatives available.

Michigan's 18-week college-planning course did not raise enrollment overall but shifted who enrolled, increasing it among stronger students and reducing it among some weaker ones, with gains in persistence.
Carr warns against simply giving advisers more discretion to judge who is 'college material,' recommending decision hygiene that breaks the choice into structured components.
quotes: But today we risk overcorrecting. The danger is replacing that overly broad default assumption with an overly confident effort to direct more students away from the path of a traditional four-year degree.

A student’s academic record can help predict whether she will complete college. But the actual choice confronting that student is different: Would attending college leave her better off than pursuing her best available alternative?
That is the false negative. Much of the post-secondary debate in recent years has focused on the first error. However, recent research suggests we should take the second type of error more seriously.

As important, the costs of the two errors may differ substantially in the long run. Sending a poorly matched student to college can mean debt, lost time, and foregone earnings. Steering away a student who would have completed can mean giving up a lifetime of higher earnings and other benefits generally associated with attaining a degree.
If prediction cannot usefully tell us which path would be better for any given individual, then we should focus instead on helping students more carefully weigh the tradeoffs involved.
But better advising should not simply mean giving high school advisors or teachers more discretion to decide who is “college material.
When uncertainty is unavoidable—which will always be the case when discussing teenagers—keeping multiple viable pathways open may be more valuable than sorting students earlier.
